description: I'm Checo Cadena, a Mexican musician and sound artist based in New York. I build interactive pieces that turn data into sound. I'm entering The Earth Information Jukebox challenge as a solo team with Earth Jukebox, an arcade machine in the browser that plays NASA's animations of the Earth as sound. My background is songwriting, sound design, Web Audio and creative coding (NYU, Berklee NYC). The project is finished, so I'm not looking for team members.
summary: Earth Jukebox plays NASA's pictures of the Earth as sound. NASA's Earth Information Center shows how the planet is changing, but almost all of it is visual, so blind and low-vision people are left out. I built an arcade machine you walk up to in the browser. Three Earths turn on its screen. One is lightning seen from the Space Station. The others are city lights at night and ocean temperature. Fly into one and it plays. The data is read straight from the frames of NASA's own animations, and each world turns it into notes in its own way. It runs from the keyboard and tells a screen reader what's playing. For people who can't hear it, captions describe the sound. NASA's original frame stays on screen next to the globe.
details:
Where the data comes from

Everything is read out of the frames of three NASA Earth Information Center animations by scripts in the tools folder. In the lightning animation, each flash is a yellow dot, so a dot that appears in one frame and wasn’t in the frame before is a new flash. That gives 2.7 million flashes with a place and a date. The animation speeds up and slows down, so the script calculates each frame's date based on how long the dots stay lit and the seasons repeating each year. For night lights, it takes one frame per year from 2012 to 2023 and keeps the small bright points. For the ocean, it takes 96 moments through one year and turns the water's color back into a temperature using NASA’s color bar. These are read from the pictures, not from the instrument files, so they show where and how much.

How it becomes sound

Every line of latitude has a note. A line near the pole is a shorter circle than the equator, so it sounds higher: the pitch is the equator’s pitch divided by the cosine of the latitude. That puts 37 degrees a major third above the equator and 60 degrees an octave above it. Night lights is a music box. The Earth is the drum and the cities are the pins, and when a city crosses the middle of the globe it plucks the note for its latitude. Lightning works the same way, with a share of the flashes plucking the note of the nearest line, so stormy months play more notes. The ocean holds a quiet chord and rings a low bell when the edge between warm and cold water crosses the middle. The Earth turns while it plays and you hear the side that’s facing you, with west in your left ear. There is reverb and an echo on all of it. The browser generates the sound with the Web Audio API. There are no samples.

What you see

White outlines on black. You start at a child’s height in front of an arcade machine, the camera rises and goes into the screen, and the three Earths orbit each other inside. Picking one flies you to it, and moving between them swings you along their orbit. The data is drawn in yellow on the globe at the same moment you hear it. NASA’s own animation appears beside the globe for the same date, and you can click it to view it larger.

Accessibility

Every action works from the keyboard, and focus is always visible. A live region tells a screen reader the date, which part of the world is facing you, and what is happening there. For deaf and hard-of-hearing visitors, the Accessibility button (or the C key) shows captions of what each sound stands for and a meter of the left and right channels. If your device is set to reduce motion, there is no camera movement and the globes stay still. Export audio saves what you hear as a WAV file.

Tools

JavaScript and the Web Audio API in the browser, with no libraries. Python scripts read the data out of NASA’s frames. The site is hosted on Netlify, and the code is public at https://github.com/checocadena/earth-jukebox.

Use of AI

I built this with Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding assistant. It wrote the code and drafted this text, which I edited. I directed it by voice and tested every version by ear and by eye. The decisions were mine: play the data itself and keep it musical, the white outline look, the arcade machine, which worlds to include. All sound is generated live by the code from NASA’s data. There is no AI-generated audio, image, video or voice in the project or the demo.
